name: Nenets
confidence_why: Salminen's grammatical sketch (1998, revised 2012) and Nikolaeva's grammar (2014) analyse Tundra Nenets stress as predictable and initial, but Amelina's instrumental studies of the Yamal, Kanin and Gydan dialects (2011, 2012) find mobile, contrastive stress on the second syllable in about half of two-syllable nouns, siding with Tereshchenko (1965) and Popova (1966, 1978), while Staroverov (2006) measures initial lengthening in the Malaya Zemlya dialect together with a lexical pitch accent, so the very type of the system is under active debate.

catalog_quote: Stress is predictable from syllable and segmental structure. It falls on an initial syllable, syllables preceding a syllable with a schwa, and non-final syllables preceded by an unstressed syllable. Stress does not fall on a final syllable (with one particular exception discussed below), syllables with a schwa, and syllables following a stressed syllable unless they precede a syllable with a schwa. Most typically, the first syllable of each two-syllable string is stressed, or in other words, the stress falls on non-final odd syllables. However, the predictability of stress holds good only if the opposition of the short vowel and the schwa is respected, because the stress relations which govern the vowel reduction are partly lexical and morphological. Taking into account those complications, the vowel reduction is an automatic phonological process where |ə| → ° in unstressed positions. .…

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog: the catalog's own domain quote for Nenets is this very passage (Salminen's sketch, section 'Stress pattern and vowel reduction'), and the sketch is the author's corrected version of the 1998 Routledge chapter, so the 1998 chapter and the catalog source are one text. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable: it falls on the initial syllable (primary stress) and then alternates onto non-final odd-numbered syllables, with the schwa vowel (°) overriding the count -- a schwa syllable is never stressed and the syllable before a schwa is always stressed; final syllables are unstressed. Only a handful of loanwords with an initial schwa (p°rasyin°, t°ronyi, x°ryís°tya) take primary stress on the second syllable. Compounds carry a separate stress pattern per member.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'the first syllable of each two-syllable string is stressed', i.e. non-primary stresses on non-final odd syllables counting from the left, plus any syllable immediately preceding a schwa syllable; a syllable following a stressed syllable is unstressed unless it precedes a schwa. Unstressed |ə| reduces to the schwa °.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Initial-schwa loanwords stress the next syllable; (ii) 'the predictability of stress holds good only if the opposition of the short vowel and the schwa is respected, because the stress relations which govern the vowel reduction are partly lexical and morphological' (cases where an unstressed schwa appears in an odd syllable after suffix-initial glides, in secondary vowel stems from liquid stems, etc.); (iii) 'one particular exception' to the ban on final-syllable stress (a post-1998 blue addition; the exception is the °xəC metathesis paragraph); (iv) compounds: each member has its own stress pattern (nye-nya : loc.sg nye-nyax°na).
new_statements.identity_note: Salminen 1998 (and its web version) describes Tundra Nenets only; the author states the printed chapter title 'Nenets' is misleading. Burkova 2022 (abstract) covers both Tundra Nenets and Forest Nenets. Künnap's review concerns the Tundra Nenets monograph. Glottolog nene1249 'Nenets' is the node over Tundra Nenets and Forest Nenets; the catalog's fixed: initial syllable record rests on Tundra Nenets (Salminen). Salminen 2007 on Forest Nenets (held by the project) also has 'stress regularly on non-final odd syllables'.

audit.recode_to: no reclassification proposed now. Keep fixed: initial syllable primary (Salminen; instrumentally supported for a Western dialect by Staroverov 2006), but add a caution documenting the competing free/lexical-stress analysis (Tereshchenko 1965: 864; Popova 1966; Amelina 2011: 10, 28-30; 2012: 44-46) and reconsider counts as exceptionless (the strict set): Salminen himself says the schwa/short-vowel stress relations are 'partly lexical and morphological', and Amelina's Eastern-dialect measurements place stress on syllable 2 in words Salminen writes without any schwa (noxa, syidya, s@wa). If the catalog codes surface prominence rather than Salminen's phonemicisation, the Eastern-dialect facts would point to 'lexical' rather than 'fixed-strict'.
